headings.title: Introduction to Systemic Circulation
headings.content: Systemic circulation is the major blood transport network of the body. It delivers oxygen-rich blood from the left side of the heart to every organ and tissue, and then returns oxygen-depleted blood back to the right side of the heart. This continuous loop supports cellular metabolism, removes metabolic wastes, and maintains overall homeostasis. Without it, tissues quickly suffer from ischemia and necrosis.

headings.title: Anatomical Pathway: Left Ventricle to the Aorta
headings.content: Blood leaves the left ventricle by forcing open the **aortic valve** and entering the **aorta**, the largest artery in the body. The aorta arches upward, gives off branches to the head and upper extremities, and descends through the thorax and abdomen to supply the lower body. The high pressure generated by the left ventricular contraction is necessary to propel blood through this vast network against gravity and peripheral resistance.

headings.title: Arterial Distribution and Microcirculation
headings.content: From the major arteries, blood travels through smaller branching vessels called **arterioles**. Arterioles regulate blood flow into the **capillaries** by constricting or dilating their smooth muscle walls. This microvascular network ensures that active tissues receive more perfusion while resting tissues receive less.

headings.title: Capillary Exchange of Nutrients and Gases
headings.content:
- **Diffusion**: Oxygen and carbon dioxide move down their concentration gradients across the single-cell capillary wall.
- **Filtration**: Hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid and dissolved solutes out of the capillary into the interstitial space.
- **Reabsorption**: Plasma proteins create osmotic pressure that pulls fluid back into the capillary near the venous end.

headings.title: Venous Return and the Vena Cavae
headings.content: After passing through the capillary beds, blood collects into venules and eventually into large veins. Because venous pressure is very low, blood relies on skeletal muscle contractions, one-way valves, and the negative pressure of breathing to return to the heart. All systemic veins ultimately drain into the **superior vena cava** and **inferior vena cava**, which empty into the right atrium.

headings.title: Hemodynamics: Blood Pressure and Peripheral Resistance
headings.content: Blood flow through the systemic circulation depends on the pressure gradient and vascular resistance. **Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)** represents the average pressure driving blood into the tissues. Resistance is determined by vessel length, blood viscosity, and especially vessel radius. Small changes in arteriolar diameter cause large changes in resistance and blood pressure.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment of Systemic Perfusion
headings.content: Nurses assess systemic circulation by evaluating vital signs and peripheral perfusion indicators. Key assessments include measuring blood pressure, checking peripheral pulses, assessing capillary refill time, and evaluating skin temperature and color. Cool, pale extremities and delayed capillary refill often signal inadequate peripheral perfusion.

headings.title: Clinical Implications of Impaired Systemic Circulation
headings.content: When systemic circulation fails, cells are deprived of oxygen and nutrients while metabolic waste accumulates. Conditions such as heart failure, hypovolemic shock, and severe atherosclerosis disrupt this vital flow. Nurses must monitor for signs of end-organ dysfunction, such as altered mental status, decreased urine output, and ischemic skin ulcers.
